item.title: Miyajidake Shrine and the Path of Light — Guide
item.description: Miyajidake Shrine in Fukutsu, between Fukuoka and Kitakyushu, is a much-loved shrine famous for several superlatives. It holds an enormous shimenawa (sacred straw rope) — one of the largest in Japan, several metres thick and weighing tonnes — along with a giant drum and bell. Its greatest fame, however, comes twice a year, in late February and late October, when the setting sun aligns perfectly with the shrine’s long, straight stone approach that runs down toward the sea, creating the spectacular ‘Path of Light’ (Hikari no Michi) — a golden road of sunlight stretching to the horizon, drawing huge crowds.

item.title: Chichibu Shrine & Old Town: A Mountain-Ringed Sacred Centre — Guide
item.description: Chichibu Shrine, with a history stretching back some 2,100 years, is one of the oldest and most revered shrines in the Kanto region, its vividly carved wooden gate and main hall set against the dramatic backdrop of the Chichibu mountains. The surrounding old town retains a quaint, small-city charm with traditional shops and eateries, serving as the spiritual and social heart of an area famous nationwide for its elaborate December night festival, one of Japan’s three great float festivals.

item.title: Kinkazan Island: Sacred Deer & Monkeys — Guide
item.description: Kinkazan — ‘Gold Flower Mountain’ — is one of Japan’s three great power spots, a sacred island off the Oshika Peninsula where hundreds of sika deer and wild macaque monkeys roam freely among the ancient shrine buildings. Koganeyama Shrine at the island’s centre has been a pilgrimage destination since the 8th century, and traditional belief holds that three consecutive January visits guarantee lifelong financial fortune. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ishinomaki (Oshika Peninsula), Miyagi Hours Ferry ~9:00–15:00 (seasonal) Admission Around ¥1,000 (island entry) Time needed About 2 hours Best time Year-round; January for the pilgrimage tradition What to See Hundreds of free-roaming sika deer and wild macaques.

item.title: Meiji Jingu Guide: Tokyo's Forest Shrine in the Heart of Harajuku
item.description: Step through the towering wooden torii at the edge of Harajuku and the city simply vanishes. Within a few paces the neon, the crowds, and the noise of Tokyo’s busiest youth district give way to a deep, hushed forest — 100,000 trees of 365 species, planted a century ago by volunteers from across Japan. At the centre stands Meiji Jingu, the Shinto shrine dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, and one of the most spiritually significant places in the capital.
